u1s0: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all forms of life or organisms.
u2s0: A biological cell basically consists of a semipermeable cell membrane enclosing cytoplasm that contains genetic material.
u3s0: Most cells are only visible under a microscope.
u4s0: Except for highly-differentiated cell types (examples include red blood cells and gametes) most cells are capable of replication, and protein synthesis.
u5s0: Some types of cell are motile.
u6s0: Cells emerged on Earth about four billion years ago.
u7s0: All multicellular organisms are made up of many different types of cell.
u8s0: The diploid cells that make up the body of a plant or animal are known as somatic cells, which excludes the haploid gametes.
u9s0: In eukaryotic cells, the nucleus is enclosed in the nuclear membrane.
u10s0: Eukaryotic cells contain other membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, which provide energy for cell functions, and chloroplasts, in plants that create sugars by photosynthesis.
u11s0: Cells were discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665, who named them after their resemblance to cells in a monastery.
u12s0: Cell theory, developed in 1839 by Matthias Jakob Schleiden and Theodor Schwann, states that all organisms are composed of one or more cells, that cells are the fundamental unit of structure and function in all organisms, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells.
u13s0: Eukaryotic cells possess a membrane-bound nucleus, and prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus but have a nucleoid region.
u14s0: Prokaryotic cells were likely the first form of life on Earth, characterized by having vital biological processes including cell signaling.
u15s0: They are simpler and smaller than eukaryotic cells, lack a nucleus, and the other usually present membrane-bound organelles.
u16s0: All prokaryotic cells secrete different substances from their membranes, including exoenzymes, and extracellular polymeric substances.
u17s0: The largest bacterium known, Thiomargarita magnifica, is visible to the naked eye with an average length of 1 cm, but can be as much as 2 cm ==== Bacteria ==== Bacteria are enclosed in a cell envelope, that protects the interior from the exterior.
u18s0: It generally consists of a plasma membrane covered by a cell wall which, for some bacteria, is covered by a third gelatinous layer called a bacterial capsule.
u19s0: Mycoplasma only possess the cell membrane.
u20s0: The cell envelope gives rigidity to the cell and separates the interior of the cell from its environment, serving as a protective mechanical and chemical filter.
u21s0: The cell wall consists of peptidoglycan and acts as an additional barrier against exterior forces.
u22s0: The cell wall acts to protect the cell mechanically and chemically from its environment, and is an additional layer of protection to the cell membrane.
u23s0: It also prevents the cell from expanding and bursting (cytolysis) from osmotic pressure due to a hypotonic environment.
u24s0: The prokaryotic cytoskeleton in bacteria is involved in the maintenance of cell shape, polarity and cytokinesis.
u25s0: Compartmentalization is a key feature of eukaryotic cells but some species of bacteria, have protein-based organelle-like microcompartments such as gas vesicles, and carboxysomes, and encapsulin nanocompartments.
u26s0: Cell-surface appendages can include flagella, and pili, protein structures that facilitate movement and communication between cells.
u27s0: The flagellum stretches from the cytoplasm through the cell membrane and extrudes through the cell wall.
u28s0: Fimbriae are formed of an antigenic protein called pilin, and are responsible for the attachment of bacteria to specific receptors on host cells.
u29s0: ==== Archaea ==== Archaea are enclosed in a cell envelope consisting of a plasma membrane and a cell wall.
u30s0: An exception to this is the Thermoplasma that only has the cell membrane.
u31s0: The cell membranes of archaea are unique, consisting of ether-linked lipids.
u32s0: Their cell-surface appendage equivalent of the flagella is the differently structured and unique archaellum.
u33s0: Ribosomes are also found freely in the cytoplasm, or attached to the cell membrane where DNA processing takes place.
u34s0: Multicellular organisms are made up of many different types of cell known overall as somatic cells.
u35s0: A eukaryotic cell can be 2 to 100 times larger in diameter than a typical prokaryotic cell.
u36s0: Eukaryotic cells have a cell membrane that surrounds a gel-like cytoplasm.
u37s0: The cytoplasm contains the cytoskeleton, and surrounds the cell nucleus, the endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, the Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes, peroxisomes, endosomes, vacuoles and vesicles, and may have a cell wall, chloroplasts, vaults, and cell-surface appendages.
u38s0: There are many cell variations among the different eukaryote groups.
u39s0: The membranes of most of the organelles including the cell membrane are sometimes referred to as the endomembrane system.
u40s0: In mammalian cells, endocytosis includes early, late, and recycling endosomes.
u41s0: Most distinct cell types arise from a single totipotent cell, called a zygote, that differentiates into hundreds of different cell types during the course of development.
u42s0: Differentiation of cells is driven by different environmental cues (such as cell–cell interaction) and intrinsic differences (such as those caused by the uneven distribution of molecules during division).
u43s0: Eukaryotic cell types include those that make up animals, plants, fungi, algae, and protists.
u44s0: All of which have many different species and cell differences.
u45s0: == Animal cells == All the cells in an animal body develop from one totipotent diploid cell called a zygote.
u46s0: During the embryonic development of an animal, the cells differentiate into the specialised tissues and organs of the organism.
u47s0: Different groups of cells differentiate from the germ layers.
u48s0: Differentiation results in structural or functional changes to stem cells, and progenitor cells.
u49s0: Epithelial cells are joined together in sheets by way of cell junctions; adherens junctions, and desmosomes bind the cells together, and hemidesmosomes bind the cells to the basement membrane.
u50s0: All three types are linked to the cell cytoskeleton.
u51s0: There are an estimated 200 different cell types in the human body.
u52s0: The estimated cell count in a typical adult human body is around 30 trillion cells, 36 trillion in an adult male, and 28 trillion in a female.
u53s0: === Structure === An animal cell has a cell membrane that surrounds a gel-like cytoplasm.
u54s0: The cytoplasm contains the cytoskeleton, the cell nucleus, the endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, the Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes, peroxisomes, endosomes, vacuoles and vesicles, and vaults.
u55s0: An animal cell structure, as other eukaryotes, includes an endomembrane system encompassing the cell membrane, and all the membranes of the organelles excluding those of the mitochondria.
u56s0: === Cell membrane === The cell membrane, or plasma membrane, is a selectively permeable membrane as an outer boundary of the cell that encloses the cytoplasm.
u57s0: The membrane serves to separate and protect a cell from its surrounding environment and is made mostly from a lipid bilayer of phospholipids, which are amphiphilic (partly hydrophobic and partly hydrophilic).
u58s0: Embedded within the cell membrane are secretory macromolecular lipoprotein structures called porosomes; and a number of different channels and pumps involved in actively transporting molecules into and out of the cell.
u59s0: Cell surface receptors in the membrane allow cells to detect external signaling molecules such as hormones. Underlying, and attached to the cell membrane is the cell cortex, the outermost part of the actin cytoskeleton. === Cytoplasm === The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm of the cell that surrounds all of the cell's organelles.
u60s0: The network of filaments and microtubules of the cytoskeleton gives shape and support to the cell, and has a part in organising the cell components.
u61s0: The acidity (pH) of the cytosol is near neutral, and is regulated by transporters in the cell membrane.
u62s0: The cytosol forms 30%–50% of the cell's volume.
u63s0: === Cytoskeleton === The cytoskeleton acts to organize and maintain the cell's shape; anchors organelles in place; helps during endocytosis, and in the uptake of external materials by a cell.
u64s0: There are a great number of proteins associated with them, each controlling a cell's structure by directing, bundling, and aligning filaments.
u65s0: The outermost part of the cytoskeleton is the cell cortex, or actin cortex, a thin layer of cross-linked actomyosins.
u66s0: Its thickness varies with cell type and physiology.
u67s0: The cytoskeleton in the animal cell also plays a part in cytokinesis, in the formation of the spindle apparatus during cell division, the separation of daughter cells.
u68s0: === Organelles === Organelles are compartments of the cell that are specialized for carrying out one or more functions, analogous to the organs, such as the heart, and lungs.
u69s0: Most organelles are membrane-bound, and vary in size and number based on the growth of the host cell.
u70s0: The cell nucleus is the largest organelle in the animal cell.
u71s0: It houses the cell's chromosomes, and is the place where almost all DNA replication and RNA synthesis (transcription) occur.
u72s0: The nuclear envelope isolates and protects a cell's DNA from various molecules that could accidentally damage its structure or interfere with its processing.
u73s0: Cells use DNA for their long-term information storage that is encoded in its DNA sequence.
u74s0: The DNA of each cell is its genetic material, and is organized in multiple linear molecules, called chromosomes, that are coiled around histone proteins and housed in the cell nucleus.
u75s0: === Golgi apparatus === The Golgi apparatus processes and packages proteins, and lipids, that are synthesized by the cell.
u76s0: === Mitochondria === Mitochondria are self-replicating double membrane-bound organelles that occur in various numbers, shapes, and sizes in the cytoplasm of the cell.
u77s0: Aerobic respiration in the mitochondria generates the cell's energy by oxidative phosphorylation, using oxygen to release energy stored in cellular nutrients (typically pertaining to glucose) to generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
u78s0: === Lysosomes === A lysosome is the most acidic compartment in the cell.
u79s0: The cell could not house these destructive enzymes if they were not contained in a membrane-bound compartment.
u80s0: They have enzymes that rid the cell of toxic peroxides.
u81s0: The peroxisomes in animal cells are concentrated in the liver cells and adipocytes.
u82s0: Some cells, most notably Amoeba, have contractile vacuoles, which can pump water out of the cell if there is too much water.
u83s0: The centrosome is the main microtubule organizing center in the animal cell that produces the microtubules key components of the cytoskeleton.
u84s0: Centrosomes are composed of two centrioles which lie perpendicular to each other in which each has an organization like a cartwheel, which separate during cell division and help in the formation of the mitotic spindle.
u85s0: Most human cells have around 10,000 vaults, and in some types of immune cell there may be up to 100,000.
u86s0: Macrophages have the greatest number of vaults of any human cell.
u87s0: They are present in normal tissues, and more so in secretory and excretory epithelial cells.
u88s0: They also function in protein homeostasis, stress response, and in the control of cell division and signal transduction.
u89s0: === Animal cell types === Some types of specialised cell are localised to a particular animal group.
u90s0: Vertebrates for example have specialised, structurally changed cells including muscle cells.
u91s0: The cell membrane of a skeletal muscle cell or of a cardiac muscle cell is termed the sarcolemma.
u92s0: Skeletal muscle cells also become multinucleated.
u93s0: The many species of vertebrates for example have other unique characteristics by way of additional specialised cells.
u94s0: In some species of electric fish for example modified muscle cells or nerve cells have specialised to become electerocytes capable of creating and storing electrical energy for future release, as in stunning prey, or use in electrolocation.
u95s0: These are large flat cells in the electric eel, and electric ray in which thousands are stacked into an electric organ comparable to a voltaic pile.
u96s0: Many animal cells are ciliated and most cells except red blood cells have primary cilia.
u97s0: Each cilium may be "viewed as a sensory cellular antennae that coordinates a large number of cellular signaling pathways, sometimes coupling the signaling to ciliary motility or alternatively to cell division and differentiation."
u98s0: The cilia in other cells are motile organelles, and in the respiratory epithelium play an important role in the movement of mucus.
u99s0: Motile cilia also known as flagella, drive the sperm cells.
u100s0: Invertebrate planarians have ciliated excretory flame cells.
u101s0: Other excretory cells also found in planarians are solenocytes that are long and flagellated.
u102s0: == Plant cells == Plant cells have cell walls composed of cellulose, hemicelluloses, and pectin that are constructed outside the cell membrane.
u103s0: In sclerenchyma tissue lignin is secreted to form a secondary wall inside the primary cell wall.
u104s0: Cutin is secreted outside the primary cell wall and into the outer layers of the secondary cell wall of the epidermal cells of leaves, stems and other above-ground organs to form the plant cuticle.
u105s0: Cell walls perform many essential functions, they provide shape to form the tissue and organs of the plant, and play an important role in intercellular communication and plant-microbe interactions.
u106s0: Specialized cell-to-cell communication pathways known as plasmodesmata, occur in the form of pores in the primary cell wall through which the cell membrane and endoplasmic reticulum of adjacent cells are continuous.
u107s0: Organelles in plant cells, include pigment-containing plastids, especially chloroplasts that contain chlorophyll (also found in algae), water-storage vacuoles, and two types of peroxisome.
u108s0: The vacuoles are larger than those in animal cells, and their membrane transports ions against concentration gradients.
u109s0: The microtubule organizing center in plant cells is often sited underneath the cell membrane where nucleated microtubules often form sheet-like semi-parallel arrays.
u110s0: Plant hormones are produced by all plant cells.
u111s0: == Algal cells == Algae members are photoautotrophs able to use photosynthesis to produce energy.
u112s0: Alginate is a polysaccharide found in the matrix of the cell walls of brown algae, and has many important uses in the food industry, and in pharmacology.
u113s0: == Fungal cells == The cells of fungi have in addition to the shared eukaryotic organelles a spitzenkörper in their endomembrane system, associated with hyphal tip growth.
u114s0: It is a phase-dark body that is composed of an aggregation of membrane-bound vesicles containing cell wall components, serving as a point of assemblage and release of such components intermediate between the Golgi and the cell membrane.
u115s0: The cell walls of fungi are uniquely made of a chitin-glucan complex.
u116s0: == Protist cells == The cells of protists may be bounded only by a cell membrane, or may in addition have a cell wall, or may be covered by a pellicle (in ciliates), a test (in testate amoebae), or a frustule (in diatoms).
u117s0: Ciliates have two different sorts of nuclei: a tiny, diploid micronucleus (the "generative nucleus", which carries the germline of the cell), and a large, ampliploid macronucleus (the "vegetative nucleus", which takes care of general cell regulation.
u118s0: == Cellular processes == === Replication === During cell division, a single cell, the mother cell divides into two daughter cells.
u119s0: Prokaryotic cells divide by binary fission, while eukaryotic cells usually undergo a process of nuclear division, called mitosis, followed by division of the cell, called cytokinesis.
u120s0: A diploid cell may undergo meiosis to produce haploid cells, usually four.
u121s0: Haploid cells serve as gametes in multicellular organisms, fusing to form new diploid cells.
u122s0: DNA replication, or the process of duplicating a cell's genome, always happens when a cell divides through mitosis or binary fission.
u123s0: This occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of the cell cycle.
u124s0: In meiosis, the DNA is replicated only once, while the cell divides twice.
u125s0: DNA replication only occurs before meiosis I. DNA replication does not occur when the cells divide the second time, in meiosis II.
u126s0: === Signaling === Cell signaling is the process by which a cell interacts with itself, other cells, and the environment.
u127s0: Most cell signaling is chemical in nature, and can occur with neighboring cells or more distant targets.
u128s0: Each cell is programmed to respond to specific extracellular signal molecules, and this process is the basis of development, tissue repair, immunity, and homeostasis.
u129s0: Individual cells are able to manage receptor sensitivity including turning them off, and receptors can become less sensitive when they are occupied for long durations.
u130s0: === Protein targeting === Protein targeting or protein sorting is the biological mechanism by which proteins are transported to their appropriate destinations within or outside the cell.
u131s0: Proteins can be targeted to the inner space of an organelle, different intracellular membranes, the plasma membrane, or to the exterior of the cell via secretion.
u132s0: Correct sorting is crucial for the cell; errors or dysfunction in sorting have been linked to multiple diseases.
u133s0: === DNA repair === All cells contain enzyme systems that scan for DNA damage and carry out repair.
u134s0: Repair is vital to maintain DNA integrity, avoid cell death and errors of replication that could lead to mutation.
u135s0: === Growth and metabolism === Between successive cell divisions, cells grow through the functioning of cellular metabolism.
u136s0: Cell metabolism is the process by which individual cells process nutrient molecules.
u137s0: Metabolism has two distinct divisions: catabolism, in which the cell breaks down complex molecules to produce energy and reducing power, and anabolism, in which the cell uses energy and reducing power to construct complex molecules and perform other biological functions.
u138s0: Once inside the cell, glucose is broken down to make adenosine triphosphate (ATP), a molecule that possesses readily available energy, through two different pathways.
u139s0: In plant cells, chloroplasts create sugars by photosynthesis, using the energy of light to join molecules of water and carbon dioxide.
u140s0: === Protein synthesis === Cells are capable of synthesizing new proteins, which are essential for the modulation and maintenance of cellular activities.
u141s0: Cells in multicellular organisms can move during processes such as wound healing, the immune response, and cancer metastasis.
u142s0: In wound healing in animals, white blood cells move to the wound site to kill the pathogens causing infection.
u143s0: Cell motility involves many receptors, crosslinking, bundling, binding, adhesion, motor and other proteins.
u144s0: The process is divided into three steps: protrusion of the leading edge of the cell, adhesion of the leading edge and de-adhesion at the cell body and rear, and cytoskeletal contraction to pull the cell forward.
u145s0: ==== Navigation, control and communication ==== In August 2020, scientists described one way cells—in particular cells of a slime mold and mouse pancreatic cancer-derived cells—are able to navigate efficiently through a body and identify the best routes through complex mazes: generating gradients after breaking down diffused chemoattractants which enable them to sense upcoming maze junctions before reaching them, including around corners.
u146s0: === Cell death === Cell death occurs when a cell ceases to carry out its functions, as a result of ageing, or types of cell injury (necrosis).
u147s0: Programmed cell death, including apoptosis, and autophagy is a natural process of replacing dead cells with new ones.
u148s0: A separate mode of cellular death is known as a mitotic catastrophe, which occurs during mitosis, following the improper progression of, or entrance to the cell cycle.
u149s0: Other cell death pathways are described, and include anoikis, pyroptosis, mitoptosis, parthanatos, and necroptosis.
u150s0: == Origins == The origin of cells has to do with the origin of life, which began the history of life on Earth.
u151s0: Cells emerged around 4 billion years ago.
u152s0: The first cells were most likely heterotrophs.
u153s0: The early cell membranes were probably simpler and more permeable than later ones, with only a single fatty acid chain per lipid.
u154s0: Eukaryotic cells were created some 2.2 billion years ago in a process called eukaryogenesis.
u155s0: This cell had a new level of complexity, with a nucleus and facultatively aerobic mitochondria.
u156s0: It featured at least one centriole and cilium, sex (meiosis and syngamy), peroxisomes, and a dormant cyst with a cell wall of chitin and/or cellulose.
u157s0: === Multicellularity === Multicellular behavior is demonstrated by microorganisms that are cloned from a single cell and form visible microbial colonies.
u158s0: Cyanobacteria are variable in morphology, filamentous forms exhibit functional cell differentiation such as heterocysts (for nitrogen fixation), akinetes (resting stage cells), and hormogonia (reproductive, motile filaments).
u159s0: EPS enables microbial cell adhesion, and is believed to be the first evolutionary step toward multicellular organisms.
u160s0: To further support his theory, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann studied cells of both animal and plants.
u161s0: What they discovered were significant differences between the two types of cells.
u162s0: This put forth the idea that cells were fundamental to both plants and animals.
u163s0: 1632–1723: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek taught himself to make lenses, constructed basic optical microscopes and drew protozoa, such as Vorticella from rain water, and bacteria from his own mouth. 1665: Robert Hooke discovered cells in cork, then in living plant tissue using an early microscope.
u164s0: In his book Micrographia he coined the term cell (from Latin cellula, meaning "small room") since they resembled the cells of a monastery 1839:
u165s0: Theodor Schwann and Matthias Jakob Schleiden elucidated the principle that plants and animals are made of cells, concluding that cells are a common unit of structure and development, founding the cell theory. 1855:
u166s0: Rudolf Virchow stated that new cells come from pre-existing cells by cell division (omnis cellula ex cellula). 1931:
u167s0: Lynn Margulis published Symbiosis in Cell Evolution detailing how eukaryotic cells were created by symbiogenesis.
